headline: Build a streaming AI chat endpoint to beat rate limits and slow responses
summary: Learn how Server-Sent Events (SSE) can transform your AI chatbot, eliminating 429 errors and providing real-time, responsive user experiences.
details: Initially, integrating OpenAI API calls into a serverless function led to frustrating 429 rate limit errors and unacceptable 5-10 second waits for chatbot responses.
Attempts to solve the problem with caching common queries or implementing a queue system with retries proved insufficient, as they didn't address the fundamental issue of blocking requests.
The core realization was that users shouldn't have to wait for the entire AI response to be generated before seeing any output. A different approach was needed to improve user experience.
The solution involved rebuilding the endpoint to stream AI responses using Server-Sent Events (SSE). This allowed each chunk of text to be sent as it arrived from the API.

This streaming method created a real-time "typing" effect for users, making the chatbot feel significantly faster even if the total processing time remained similar. It also enabled early stream cancellation, reducing unnecessary API calls.
The implementation utilized a simplified Node.js Express endpoint that proxied streaming from the OpenAI API (with `stream: true`) and the EventSource API on the frontend for listening to events.
The technique proved provider-agnostic, successfully tested with a local Ollama instance and other OpenAI-compatible API endpoints, offering flexibility for development and prototyping.

Building this streaming AI endpoint provided valuable lessons beyond just SSE, emphasizing the importance of considering connection lifecycles, error resilience, and overall user experience in AI application development.
caption:
Struggling with OpenAI API rate limits and slow AI chatbot responses? Discover how to build a streaming endpoint that delivers real-time answers.

Initially, integrating OpenAI API calls into a serverless function led to frustrating 429 rate limit errors and unacceptable 5-10 second waits for chatbot responses.

Attempts to solve the problem with caching common queries or implementing a queue system with retries proved insufficient, as they didn't address the fundamental issue of blocking requests.

The core realization was that users shouldn't have to wait for the entire AI response to be generated before seeing any output. A different approach was needed to improve user experience.

The solution involved rebuilding the endpoint to stream AI responses using Server-Sent Events (SSE). This allowed each chunk of text to be sent as it arrived from the API.

This streaming method created a real-time "typing" effect for users, making the chatbot feel significantly faster even if the total processing time remained similar. It also enabled early stream cancellation, reducing unnecessary API calls.

The implementation utilized a simplified Node.js Express endpoint that proxied streaming from the OpenAI API (with `stream: true`) and the EventSource API on the frontend for listening to events.

The technique proved provider-agnostic, successfully tested with a local Ollama instance and other OpenAI-compatible API endpoints, offering flexibility for development and prototyping.

Building this streaming AI endpoint provided valuable lessons beyond just SSE, emphasizing the importance of considering connection lifecycles, error resilience, and overall user experience in AI application development.

headline_marked: [[Tesla driver faces manslaughter charges]] after crash killed woman in her home, FSD claimed
headline: Tesla driver faces manslaughter charges after crash killed woman in her home, FSD claimed
summary: Michael Butler was arrested after his Model 3, allegedly using Full Self-Driving, crashed into a Texas home, killing 76-year-old Martha Avila. Police found data suggesting Butler's recent frustration with FSD's 'timid' behavior.
details: A 44-year-old Tesla driver, Michael Butler, has been arrested and is now facing manslaughter charges after his vehicle struck and killed a woman inside her Texas home last month. Butler claimed he was driving his Model 3 using Tesla’s Full-Self Driving (FSD) system at the time of the fatal crash.

An arrest affidavit revealed that data extracted from Butler’s phone showed multiple Google searches from May 2026, indicating frustration with FSD. Searches included phrases like “Tesla fsd not aggressive enough” and “FSD is not aggressive enough for city driving.”

On June 19th, 76-year-old Martha Avila died when Butler's Tesla plowed through her home in Katy, Texas. Tesla AI head Ashok Elluswamy initially tweeted that the driver "manually overrode self-driving by pressing the accelerator all the way to 100%."

Avila's family has since filed a wrongful death lawsuit against both Tesla and Butler. Federal agencies, including the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), have launched independent investigations into the incident.

According to the affidavit, Butler told paramedics that the car was on 'autopilot' and he remembered changing music and looking at the navigation screen before the collision. He also told hospital providers he 'passed out' after putting the car in self-driving mode; however, an evaluation found no alcohol or drugs in his system.

Officials reviewed video from Butler’s Model 3 and data from the vehicle’s 'black box,' concluding that the accelerator pedal was pressed, overriding FSD’s speed control. The video showed Butler's Tesla accelerating to 73 mph, more than double the residential speed limit, with the accelerator pedal pressed 100% in the six seconds before impact, and the brake pedal was never pressed.
